questions.question: A patient investigated for ventricular ectopy has a normal-sized LV and LVEF 57%. CMR shows definite nonischemic myocardial scar. Coronary and loading-condition assessment does not explain the findings. Which ESC 2023 phenotype best describes this presentation?
options: Restrictive cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy
Non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation:
Non-Dilated Left Ventricular Cardiomyopathy

Correct answer: Non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy

Classify the Observed Phenotype Before Naming the Cause

**Non-dilated LV cardiomyopathy can be present despite preserved global EF.** ESC 2023 includes unexplained nonischemic LV scar or fatty replacement without LV dilatation, with or without regional or global motion abnormalities.

The category also includes isolated global LV hypokinesia without scar when abnormal loading conditions or coronary disease do not adequately explain it. It is broader than a requirement for both scar and reduced EF.

Measure ventricular dimensions and function using appropriate body-size and sex context. A report of normal EF does not answer whether tissue disease or a regional functional abnormality exists.

Move From Phenotype to Etiology and Risk

**A cardiomyopathy phenotype is the beginning of etiological assessment.** Review the pedigree, conduction and arrhythmic features, exposures, inflammatory presentations, extracardiac findings and CMR distribution.

Inherited disease and prior inflammatory injury are possible explanations. Do not declare myocarditis, a particular gene or inevitable malignant arrhythmia from a nonischemic LGE pattern alone.

Assess symptoms, ambulatory rhythm data and family history alongside scar and ventricular function. Some genetic substrates carry arrhythmic risk before marked EF reduction, but scar alone is not a universal ICD mandate. Treat documented HF or arrhythmia according to the established problem, arrange phenotype-directed genetic counseling where appropriate and reassess over time. A normal chamber size must not end investigation when reproducible tissue abnormalities are present. Conversely, an equivocal enhancement focus needs expert confirmation before assigning a lifelong inherited diagnosis.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterized by restrictive ventricular physiology and the relevant structural-functional phenotype. Nonischemic scar alone does not establish restricted filling or that classification.

Dilated cardiomyopathy: DCM requires LV dilatation with systolic dysfunction not explained solely by loading conditions or coronary disease. A normal-sized LV with preserved global EF does not meet that phenotype.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: HCM requires otherwise unexplained increased ventricular wall thickness. Scar can accompany HCM but cannot substitute for the absent hypertrophic phenotype in this case.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

questions.question: CMR performed for an unrelated indication shows prominent LV trabeculation. Ventricular size and function are normal, there is no scar or thrombus, and history, ECG and family assessment are reassuring. Which interpretation best follows ESC 2023 classification?
options: A basis for predictive family genotyping before establishing a familial cause
An imaging-defined cardiomyopathy based on the trabecular appearance alone
A basis for preventive anticoagulation despite sinus rhythm and no thrombus
A morphological trait requiring interpretation within the overall clinical phenotype
questions.explanation:
Left Ventricular Hypertrabeculation

Correct answer: A morphological trait requiring interpretation within the overall clinical phenotype

Separate a Morphological Descriptor From Disease

**ESC 2023 treats LV hypertrabeculation as a phenotypic trait rather than a cardiomyopathy category in its own right.** It can occur alone, with developmental abnormalities, or with a defined hypertrophic or dilated phenotype.

The older term LV noncompaction can encourage an unsupported assumption that an imaging ratio establishes a single embryological disease. Different imaging definitions identify overlapping populations rather than one uniform prognosis.

Physiological or acquired prominence can be seen in pregnancy and athletic adaptation. The assessment must still distinguish that context from dysfunction, scar, a familial phenotype or a syndromic disorder.

Base Management on the Associated Clinical Abnormalities

**Assess ventricular function, arrhythmia, thrombus, embolic history and familial or extracardiac evidence.** Those findings determine investigation and treatment more directly than trabecular prominence alone.

Anticoagulation is considered for established indications such as AF with the relevant risk context or documented ventricular thrombus. An isolated reassuring trabecular appearance is not a universal indication for anticoagulation or an ICD.

When dysfunction or concerning arrhythmia accompanies the morphology, investigate the cardiomyopathy rather than dismissing it as a normal variant. Use expert image review if apical visualization or measurement is uncertain, and individualize follow-up according to the wider phenotype. A normal present evaluation is reassuring but should be revisited if syncope, ventricular dysfunction or a new familial diagnosis appears. Explain the finding in proportion to the evidence so an anatomical descriptor is not mistaken for proof of inevitable HF or sudden death.

A basis for predictive family genotyping before establishing a familial cause: A defined cardiomyopathy or suggestive family phenotype can justify genetic evaluation. Isolated trabeculation does not identify a causal variant for meaningful predictive cascade testing in healthy relatives.

An imaging-defined cardiomyopathy based on the trabecular appearance alone: Older LV noncompaction labels can suggest a standalone disease from morphology. ESC 2023 instead treats hypertrabeculation as a trait; the reassuring function, tissue assessment and history do not supply an associated cardiomyopathy phenotype.

A basis for preventive anticoagulation despite sinus rhythm and no thrombus: Thromboembolism is important when hypertrabeculation accompanies AF, thrombus or other relevant risk. The isolated reassuring trait does not itself establish that anticoagulation benefit exceeds bleeding risk.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

questions.question: CMR in a patient with unexplained LV dysfunction shows linear midwall septal late gadolinium enhancement, sparing the subendocardium. Which imaging mechanism directly accounts for the abnormal delayed postcontrast signal?
options: Retention of extracellular contrast in tissue with an expanded distribution space
Iron-related susceptibility causing a reduction in myocardial T2-star
Intracellular lipid storage producing a reduction in native myocardial T1
Increased tissue water identified directly by a myocardial T2 map
questions.explanation:
Late Gadolinium Enhancement in Cardiomyopathy Evaluation

Correct answer: Retention of extracellular contrast in tissue with an expanded distribution space

Contrast Distribution and Delayed Enhancement

**Conventional gadolinium agents distribute in the extracellular compartment, and expanded distribution space or altered washout produces late enhancement.** Fibrosis, necrotic injury and some infiltrative processes can create that contrast difference.

LGE is distinct from native T1, T2 or T2-star mapping. The sequences answer related but different tissue questions, so their findings should not be treated as interchangeable.

Acute tissue injury and chronic fibrosis can both enhance. The signal mechanism does not by itself identify the cause or establish that inflammation is currently active.

Interpret Distribution Alongside Function and Edema

**LGE distribution provides etiological clues rather than an isolated molecular or histological diagnosis.** Subendocardial or transmural enhancement in a vascular territory supports ischemic injury; midwall or subepicardial patterns commonly support nonischemic injury.

Septal midwall fibrosis is encountered in DCM, while inferolateral subepicardial injury can occur after myocarditis and in inherited substrates. Patterns overlap and do not eliminate the need to consider coronary disease when otherwise clinically plausible.

T2-based edema assessment and T1-based injury findings contribute to myocarditis evaluation. Persistent enhancement can remain after acute inflammation resolves; LGE is not synonymous with ongoing viral replication or steroid-responsive disease.

Use CMR to Refine Etiology and Prognosis

**Integrate the scan with the clinical course, ECG, biomarkers, coronary evaluation and family history.** CMR can identify occult scar despite a relatively preserved EF or an initially unrevealing echocardiogram.

Scar can provide an arrhythmic substrate and add prognostic information, but the effect depends on disease, distribution, burden and the wider risk profile. Do not convert any positive LGE finding into an automatic device indication.

Consider expert review when artefact, incomplete myocardial nulling or unusual distribution makes interpretation uncertain. Diffuse interstitial disease may be better characterized using mapping and extracellular-volume assessment than focal enhancement alone. Conversely, absent LGE does not exclude every genetic cardiomyopathy or an early inflammatory process. Select further testing to answer a defined question, such as genetic cause, active inflammation or an infiltrative subtype, rather than treating the scan as a replacement for the whole diagnostic pathway.

Iron-related susceptibility causing a reduction in myocardial T2-star: Iron loading is assessed using susceptibility-sensitive T2-star measurements and can cause cardiomyopathy. It is not the mechanism of regional delayed gadolinium retention described here.

Intracellular lipid storage producing a reduction in native myocardial T1: Low native T1 can provide a storage-disease clue, particularly in Fabry disease. That precontrast tissue property is distinct from the mechanism of delayed extracellular contrast enhancement.

Increased tissue water identified directly by a myocardial T2 map: T2 mapping assesses edema and can complement LGE when investigating inflammation. It is a different measurement, and late enhancement alone does not directly establish active edema.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

ESC myocarditis and pericarditis guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192

ACCF/ACR/AHA/NASCI/SCMR cardiovascular magnetic resonance consensus, 2010 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0b013e3181d44a8f

questions.question: A heterozygous parent has a confirmed pathogenic autosomal dominant sarcomeric variant. The other parent does not carry it. Which statement correctly describes counseling for each child?
options: Each child has a fifty-percent transmission probability, while clinical expression and severity remain variable
Each child has a twenty-five-percent transmission probability because the disorder may be silent
Each child inherits the variant, but only half develop disease
Only children with an abnormal ECG can have inherited the variant
questions.explanation:
Autosomal Dominant Cardiomyopathy and Penetrance

Correct answer: Each child has a fifty-percent transmission probability, while clinical expression and severity remain variable

Distinguish Transmission, Penetrance and Expressivity

**A heterozygous autosomal dominant variant has a one-half probability of transmission in each pregnancy.** Previous children’s results do not change that independent probability.

Penetrance describes whether a carrier manifests the phenotype, often in an age-dependent manner. Expressivity describes the form and severity of manifestations among affected carriers.

The same familial variant can be associated with different wall thickness, conduction disease, ventricular function or arrhythmic history. A parent’s current mild phenotype does not guarantee a similarly mild course for every carrier child.

Use Counseling to Guide Testing and Surveillance

**Offer appropriately counseled targeted testing when a reliable familial pathogenic or likely pathogenic result is available.** Timing in children depends on the disease, family presentation and whether results change childhood surveillance or care.

A genotype-positive relative with normal initial imaging can need continued phenotype surveillance. A negative result for the established familial cause has a different meaning from a negative broad panel in an affected proband.

Do not assume all cardiomyopathies follow autosomal dominant inheritance. X-linked, recessive, mitochondrial and syndromic conditions require their own counseling. Review the validity of the gene–disease association and the variant classification before giving predictive advice. Discuss reproductive choices and family communication without predicting inevitable disability from genotype alone. New symptoms require evaluation even during a scheduled surveillance interval, and variant interpretation may need review as evidence changes. Clinical care follows the relevant phenotype and risk rather than transmission probability alone.

Each child has a twenty-five-percent transmission probability because the disorder may be silent: Twenty-five-percent affected risk describes a typical autosomal recessive carrier-pair situation. Reduced penetrance changes expression after inheritance, not the one-half transmission probability from this heterozygous parent.

Each child inherits the variant, but only half develop disease: That confuses transmission with penetrance. One-half transmission applies to each pregnancy; penetrance among carriers is a separate, age- and variant-dependent question.

Only children with an abnormal ECG can have inherited the variant: Clinical manifestations can be delayed or incomplete. A normal ECG cannot establish absence of a known familial pathogenic variant in an otherwise at-risk child.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS genetic testing consensus, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1002/joa3.12717

questions.question: A DCM proband has a variant of uncertain significance in a plausible disease gene. An asymptomatic sister asks for a predictive test so a negative result can end cardiac surveillance. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Treat the VUS as benign and end evaluation of the whole family
Use targeted VUS testing and discharge the sister if negative
Diagnose cardiomyopathy in the sister if the VUS is present
Do not use the VUS as a definitive predictive test; arrange clinical family screening and specialist variant review
questions.explanation:
A Variant of Uncertain Significance in Cardiomyopathy

Correct answer: Do not use the VUS as a definitive predictive test; arrange clinical family screening and specialist variant review

Uncertainty Is a Classification With Clinical Consequences

**A VUS is not a pathogenic or likely pathogenic result.** A plausible gene name and an uncommon DNA change are insufficient to establish that the variant explains the cardiomyopathy.

Review the gene–disease validity, phenotype fit, population frequency and available segregation or functional evidence through an experienced cardiovascular genetics service. Do not independently upgrade the report based on one suggestive clinical similarity.

Testing selected informative affected relatives can help determine segregation and eventual reclassification. This is different from using the finding as a validated predictive test in a healthy relative.

Continue Phenotype-Based Family Care

**Clinical screening can remain indicated because the familial cause is unresolved.** History, examination, ECG and cardiac imaging assess disease rather than the uncertain molecular label.

A normal initial evaluation does not necessarily eliminate future expression in an at-risk family. Follow-up depends on age, phenotype, family history and the specialist plan.

Arrange a mechanism for updated interpretation rather than leaving the VUS permanently treated as either disease-causing or harmless. If it is later reclassified with adequate evidence, appropriately counseled cascade testing may become informative. ICD treatment, drug prescriptions and exercise restrictions should not be triggered solely by VUS carriage. Conversely, an affected sister would require clinical care even if she lacked this uncertain finding. Explain why a reassuring-looking targeted result cannot answer the family’s risk question until the variant’s causal role is established.

Treat the VUS as benign and end evaluation of the whole family: Uncertain is not equivalent to benign. The proband’s disease and pedigree can still justify clinical family screening while the molecular finding remains unresolved.

Use targeted VUS testing and discharge the sister if negative: Predictive exclusion requires a sufficiently established familial causal variant. Absence of an uncertain finding does not reliably exclude the unknown familial cause of this DCM.

Diagnose cardiomyopathy in the sister if the VUS is present: Presence of a VUS does not establish pathogenicity or a clinical phenotype. Overclassification can lead to unnecessary restrictions, treatment and anxiety.

questions.explanationHtml:
A Variant of Uncertain Significance in Cardiomyopathy

Correct answer: D — Do not use the VUS as a definitive predictive test; arrange clinical family screening and specialist variant review

Uncertainty Is a Classification With Clinical Consequences

  • A VUS is not a pathogenic or likely pathogenic result. A plausible gene name and an uncommon DNA change are insufficient to establish that the variant explains the cardiomyopathy.
    • Review the gene–disease validity, phenotype fit, population frequency and available segregation or functional evidence through an experienced cardiovascular genetics service. Do not independently upgrade the report based on one suggestive clinical similarity.
    • Testing selected informative affected relatives can help determine segregation and eventual reclassification. This is different from using the finding as a validated predictive test in a healthy relative.

Continue Phenotype-Based Family Care

  • Clinical screening can remain indicated because the familial cause is unresolved. History, examination, ECG and cardiac imaging assess disease rather than the uncertain molecular label.
    • A normal initial evaluation does not necessarily eliminate future expression in an at-risk family. Follow-up depends on age, phenotype, family history and the specialist plan.
    • Arrange a mechanism for updated interpretation rather than leaving the VUS permanently treated as either disease-causing or harmless. If it is later reclassified with adequate evidence, appropriately counseled cascade testing may become informative. ICD treatment, drug prescriptions and exercise restrictions should not be triggered solely by VUS carriage. Conversely, an affected sister would require clinical care even if she lacked this uncertain finding. Explain why a reassuring-looking targeted result cannot answer the family’s risk question until the variant’s causal role is established.

Other Options

  • A — Treat the VUS as benign and end evaluation of the whole family: Uncertain is not equivalent to benign. The proband’s disease and pedigree can still justify clinical family screening while the molecular finding remains unresolved.
  • B — Use targeted VUS testing and discharge the sister if negative: Predictive exclusion requires a sufficiently established familial causal variant. Absence of an uncertain finding does not reliably exclude the unknown familial cause of this DCM.
  • C — Diagnose cardiomyopathy in the sister if the VUS is present: Presence of a VUS does not establish pathogenicity or a clinical phenotype. Overclassification can lead to unnecessary restrictions, treatment and anxiety.

questions.explanation:
Interpreting a Negative Cascade Genetic Test

Correct answer: End routine surveillance for the established familial variant, with return for symptoms or revised family information

Ask Whether the Negative Result Is Informative

**Targeted cascade testing is most useful after identifying a convincing familial pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant.** In an otherwise reassuring relative, absence of that cause can remove the need for repeated surveillance directed at it.

Confirm that the family’s disease is adequately explained and that no additional causal variant or separate phenotype is known. Complex pedigrees, an affected test-negative relative or uncertain causality require reassessment rather than automatic discharge.

Do not extend the same conclusion to a VUS or to an affected proband with no finding on a broad panel. Current testing does not detect every genetic mechanism.

Combine Molecular Results With Clinical Findings

**An abnormal clinical phenotype needs investigation even when targeted familial testing is negative.** Another cause or a more complex familial explanation may be present.

A genotype-positive, phenotype-negative relative has the converse problem: clinical expression may emerge later, so disease-specific surveillance can remain necessary. Neither group should be managed by family history alone without interpreting the actual result.

Document the result and the reason for the follow-up plan, and advise review for syncope, exertional symptoms, sustained palpitations or new family information. Discuss implications for descendants with genetic counseling; a relative who does not carry the variant cannot transmit that variant through the tested family line. This is a specific statement about the established familial cause, not a guarantee against coronary disease, hypertension or other future cardiac problems. Revisit the plan if the original molecular classification changes.

Order a broad cardiomyopathy panel before interpreting the targeted negative: Broad testing can be useful when an unexplained phenotype or complex family evidence remains. It is not routinely needed to validate an informative negative in this reassuring relative and can introduce uncertain findings.

Continue the same serial screening used for a genotype-positive relative: Continued surveillance is appropriate for a carrier or when familial causality remains unresolved. Here the established cause is excluded and the clinical assessment is normal, so retaining the carrier schedule is generally unnecessary.

Discharge the relative but retain familial-variant surveillance for all their children: A person who does not carry the established familial variant cannot transmit it. Routine surveillance of descendants for that same familial cause is generally unnecessary unless another clinical or family concern emerges.

questions.question: An adult first-degree relative of a patient with unequivocal HCM has maximal end-diastolic LV wall thickness 14 mm, measured reliably. There is no hypertension, valve disease or other adequate loading explanation. Which interpretation fits ESC 2023 diagnostic criteria?
options: HCM requires resting outflow obstruction in addition to the wall thickness
HCM is excluded because every adult requires at least fifteen millimeters
The familial adult wall-thickness threshold is met; fifteen millimeters is not required in this context
HCM requires a positive genetic test in addition to the familial imaging finding
questions.explanation:
Adult Diagnostic Wall-Thickness Thresholds in HCM

Correct answer: The familial adult wall-thickness threshold is met; fifteen millimeters is not required in this context

Interpret Thickness in the Appropriate Population

**ESC defines adult HCM by maximal LV wall thickness of at least ==15 mm== not explained solely by loading conditions.** In adult first-degree relatives of unequivocal disease, at least ==13 mm== can establish the clinical hypertrophic phenotype.

A borderline measurement outside that familial setting needs additional evidence, such as the pedigree, ECG, molecular findings and morphology. Do not interpret thirteen millimeters as a universal threshold for every adult.

Pediatric assessment uses body-size-adjusted measurements and the appropriate clinical framework. Applying an unadjusted adult millimeter cut-off to a small child can misclassify disease.

Confirm Measurement and Exclude Phenocopies

**Measure maximal end-diastolic thickness across the LV rather than assuming the basal septum is the only relevant segment.** CMR can resolve poor echo windows and identify apical or other focal hypertrophy.

Exclude inclusion of RV structures, trabeculae or oblique imaging in the measurement. Hypertension can coexist with HCM, so the question is whether loading conditions adequately explain the magnitude and pattern.

Evaluate amyloid, Fabry and other storage or syndromic conditions when clinical clues suggest them; unexplained thickness is a phenotype, not proof of a sarcomere defect. Once HCM is supported, assess symptoms, LVOT gradients, atrial arrhythmia and sudden-death risk rather than basing treatment solely on the diagnostic threshold. Family genetic counseling and appropriate screening remain relevant even when the proband’s panel is negative. A fourteen-millimeter familial diagnosis does not independently establish an indication for septal reduction or an ICD.

Adult setting under ESC 2023 | Wall-thickness interpretation

Unexplained hypertrophy in an adult | ==≥15 mm== in any LV myocardial segment

First-degree relative of unequivocal HCM | ==≥13 mm== can meet the familial criterion

Borderline thickness outside that context | Integrate loading conditions, family, ECG and genetic evidence

HCM requires resting outflow obstruction in addition to the wall thickness: Obstruction is a functional subclassification, not a requirement for HCM diagnosis. Many affected patients have nonobstructive disease or develop obstruction only with provocation.

HCM is excluded because every adult requires at least fifteen millimeters: The usual unexplained adult threshold is fifteen millimeters, but adult first-degree relatives of unequivocally affected patients have a lower thirteen-millimeter threshold in the specified framework.

HCM requires a positive genetic test in addition to the familial imaging finding: Genetics can clarify cause and family testing, but clinical diagnostic criteria do not require finding a pathogenic variant in every otherwise qualifying affected relative.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

questions.question: A patient with established HCM has a resting peak instantaneous LVOT gradient of 36 mmHg and a provoked gradient of 43 mmHg. Which interpretation correctly separates classification from the threshold usually used to consider advanced obstruction-directed treatment?
options: Resting obstructive HCM, below the usual gradient threshold for advanced treatment assessment
Nonobstructive HCM, because the maximum documented gradient is below fifty
Resting obstructive HCM, already meeting the usual gradient criterion for septal reduction
Latent obstructive HCM, because only the provoked measurement qualifies as obstruction
questions.explanation:
LV Outflow Obstruction: Definition and Treatment Threshold

Correct answer: Resting obstructive HCM, below the usual gradient threshold for advanced treatment assessment

Use Two Thresholds for Two Different Questions

**A peak instantaneous Doppler LVOT gradient of at least ==30 mmHg== at rest or with physiological provocation defines obstruction.** A gradient of at least ==50 mmHg== is generally the level used when considering advanced drugs or septal reduction for persistent attributable symptoms.

The gradient is dynamic. Preload, afterload, contractility, heart rate and activity can change its magnitude, so one resting value does not fully describe an individual’s exertional physiology.

Document the measurement conditions and examine systolic anterior mitral motion and associated mitral regurgitation. Avoid mistaking a high-velocity MR jet for the outflow signal.

Link Hemodynamics to Symptoms and Treatment

**Neither numerical threshold alone establishes an indication for an invasive procedure.** Assess symptom burden, the relationship to obstruction, prior therapy, anatomy and patient preferences.

Physiological provocation and exercise echocardiography can reveal clinically relevant latent obstruction when resting or simple provoked gradients are below fifty. Doppler gradients should not be substituted directly for a catheter peak-to-peak measurement.

Initial symptomatic obstructive management commonly uses a nonvasodilating beta blocker, with suitable alternatives and escalation assessed individually. Persistent symptoms with adequate obstruction can prompt consideration of a myosin inhibitor, disopyramide or septal reduction in an experienced service. If symptoms appear disproportionate to a modest gradient, investigate diastolic dysfunction, ischemia, AF, pulmonary disease and other contributors rather than adding rest and provoked numbers. Repeat assessment under relevant conditions when symptoms change. This patient meets the definition of obstruction but the supplied measurements do not by themselves meet the usual advanced-treatment gradient threshold.

Nonobstructive HCM, because the maximum documented gradient is below fifty: The definition of obstruction uses thirty millimeters of mercury, not fifty. A resting gradient of thirty-six meets that definition even though it is below the usual advanced-treatment threshold.

Resting obstructive HCM, already meeting the usual gradient criterion for septal reduction: Resting obstruction is correctly recognized, but the usual intervention gradient is at least fifty with relevant symptoms and suitable anatomy. Neither supplied measurement reaches that hemodynamic threshold.

Latent obstructive HCM, because only the provoked measurement qualifies as obstruction: Latent obstruction describes a qualifying provoked gradient when resting obstruction is absent. Here the resting value already exceeds thirty, so the disease is obstructive at rest.

questions.question: A patient with confirmed HCM has reproducible exertional dyspnea and near-syncope. Resting LVOT gradient is 18 mmHg and Valsalva produces 28 mmHg. There is no acute illness or unstable rhythm. Which investigation best assesses whether dynamic obstruction explains the exertional symptoms?
options: Resting contrast-enhanced CMR
Dobutamine stress echocardiography
Supervised exercise echocardiography with LVOT assessment
Coronary CT angiography
questions.explanation:
Exercise Echocardiography for Latent LVOT Obstruction

Correct answer: Supervised exercise echocardiography with LVOT assessment

Reproduce the Relevant Physiology

**Exercise echocardiography is recommended in symptomatic HCM when resting and simple provoked testing do not reveal a gradient of at least ==50 mmHg==.** It can identify latent obstruction and relate it to the patient’s symptoms.

Standing and Valsalva are useful initial provocative maneuvers, but a negative or modest response does not exclude exercise-associated obstruction. Dynamic gradients change with preload, afterload, heart rate and contractility.

Record the gradient under the protocol’s exercise and recovery conditions, symptoms, blood-pressure response and rhythm. Interpretation should distinguish the LVOT signal from mitral regurgitation and identify the mechanism of obstruction.

Choose Each Test for the Question It Can Answer

**A physiological provoked gradient is interpreted alongside symptoms and anatomy.** It is not interchangeable with an isolated pharmacological response or proof that obstruction explains every complaint.

CMR remains valuable for poorly visualized hypertrophy, apical disease, scar and risk assessment. Coronary evaluation is appropriate when ischemic symptoms, age or risk factors create that separate question.

Use supervision and rescue capability appropriate to the patient’s history; exercise testing is not an unsupervised challenge for someone with unstable symptoms. Persistent exertional limitation without a significant gradient warrants assessment of diastolic dysfunction, microvascular ischemia, AF, chronotropic limitation, pulmonary disease or other contributors. A newly demonstrated gradient of at least fifty can support advanced obstruction-directed assessment when symptoms remain important despite suitable treatment, but does not independently establish a septal procedure indication. Document both the resting and provoked results so later treatment decisions reflect the actual hemodynamic context.

Resting contrast-enhanced CMR: CMR characterizes morphology, scar and alternative diagnoses, but a resting study does not reproduce the dynamic loading and contractile conditions causing the supplied exertional symptoms.

Dobutamine stress echocardiography: Dobutamine can provoke obstruction through nonphysiological inotropic stimulation. Exercise is the preferred physiological approach for this symptom–gradient question rather than using an artificial drug-induced peak as the clinical surrogate.

Coronary CT angiography: Coronary CT can investigate suspected coronary disease in an appropriate patient. It does not replace Doppler assessment of the changing outflow gradient during physiological exercise.

Record the gradient under the protocol’s exercise and recovery conditions, symptoms, blood-pressure response and rhythm. Interpretation should distinguish the LVOT signal from mitral regurgitation and identify the mechanism of obstruction.

sections.heading: Choose Each Test for the Question It Can Answer

bullets.text: **A physiological provoked gradient is interpreted alongside symptoms and anatomy.** It is not interchangeable with an isolated pharmacological response or proof that obstruction explains every complaint.
children: CMR remains valuable for poorly visualized hypertrophy, apical disease, scar and risk assessment. Coronary evaluation is appropriate when ischemic symptoms, age or risk factors create that separate question.

Use supervision and rescue capability appropriate to the patient’s history; exercise testing is not an unsupervised challenge for someone with unstable symptoms. Persistent exertional limitation without a significant gradient warrants assessment of diastolic dysfunction, microvascular ischemia, AF, chronotropic limitation, pulmonary disease or other contributors. A newly demonstrated gradient of at least fifty can support advanced obstruction-directed assessment when symptoms remain important despite suitable treatment, but does not independently establish a septal procedure indication. Document both the resting and provoked results so later treatment decisions reflect the actual hemodynamic context.

otherOptions.explanation: CMR characterizes morphology, scar and alternative diagnoses, but a resting study does not reproduce the dynamic loading and contractile conditions causing the supplied exertional symptoms.

Dobutamine can provoke obstruction through nonphysiological inotropic stimulation. Exercise is the preferred physiological approach for this symptom–gradient question rather than using an artificial drug-induced peak as the clinical surrogate.
Coronary CT can investigate suspected coronary disease in an appropriate patient. It does not replace Doppler assessment of the changing outflow gradient during physiological exercise.

questions.question: A competitive endurance athlete has borderline LV wall thickening on screening. Which additional finding would most strongly increase concern for HCM rather than uncomplicated athletic remodeling?
options: A concordant family history with focal asymmetric hypertrophy and nonischemic scar
Balanced biventricular enlargement with preserved functional reserve
Regression of wall thickening after an adequate period of detraining
Isolated sinus bradycardia with otherwise reassuring examination and imaging
questions.explanation:
Athletic Remodeling Versus Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

Correct answer: A concordant family history with focal asymmetric hypertrophy and nonischemic scar

Use Convergent Evidence in the Borderline Zone

**Borderline wall thickness in an athlete requires integrated assessment rather than a single imaging cut-off.** Training type, sex, body size, ancestry, loading conditions and measurement quality affect interpretation.

A concerning pedigree, focal or asymmetric hypertrophy, impaired relaxation, unexpected ECG abnormalities and disease-pattern scar increase suspicion. No single finding has perfect sensitivity or specificity.

Physiological endurance remodeling often includes proportionate chamber enlargement and preserved reserve. However, athletic participation does not prevent inherited disease, and an athletic-looking chamber does not overrule a strongly abnormal family or tissue assessment.

Resolve Uncertainty Before Giving Definitive Advice

**CMR can clarify morphology, apical involvement, scar and alternative diagnoses.** Review the complete ECG and consider appropriate ambulatory and exercise assessment rather than labeling every repolarization variant pathological.

Detraining can provide supportive information when feasible, but neither a short incomplete trial nor absent regression alone proves HCM. Interpret a pathogenic molecular finding through the phenotype; a VUS is not diagnostic.

Counsel through an experienced sports-cardiology or HCM service when the distinction remains uncertain. If HCM is established, participation decisions require current individualized risk assessment and shared discussion, rather than an automatic assumption that all exercise is prohibited. If evaluation supports physiological adaptation, explain the evidence and any follow-up triggers. Syncope, new exertional symptoms, progressive structural change or new familial information should prompt reassessment. The supplied answer is strongest because independent familial, morphological and tissue findings converge, not because asymmetry or any small enhancement focus alone conclusively identifies a sarcomeric disorder.

Balanced biventricular enlargement with preserved functional reserve: Proportionate enlargement and an appropriate exercise response can accompany endurance adaptation. They do not exclude disease by themselves, but are less concerning than the convergent familial and focal tissue findings.

Regression of wall thickening after an adequate period of detraining: Reversal supports a training-related component. Lack of complete regression is not a standalone HCM criterion, but documented regression is less supportive of fixed pathological hypertrophy than the proposed familial scar phenotype.

Isolated sinus bradycardia with otherwise reassuring examination and imaging: Resting bradycardia can reflect athletic autonomic adaptation. Without a concerning electrical, structural or family context it is a weaker disease marker than focal hypertrophy with scar and an affected pedigree.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

AHA/ACC multisociety hypertrophic cardiomyopathy guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.014

questions.question: An adult has marked precordial T-wave inversion and persistent clinical suspicion of apical HCM. Routine echo shows preserved EF but the apex is foreshortened and poorly defined. CMR is feasible. Which investigation most directly resolves the remaining structural question?
options: Invasive left ventriculography
Transesophageal echocardiography
CMR with complete apical morphology and tissue characterization
Exercise stress echocardiography
questions.explanation:
Imaging Suspected Apical Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

Correct answer: CMR with complete apical morphology and tissue characterization

Inspect the Entire Ventricle

**Apical HCM can be missed when the apex is foreshortened or inadequately visualized.** Preserved global EF and a normal basal septal measurement do not exclude regional hypertrophy.

CMR defines apical thickness, cavity shape, scar and possible aneurysm or thrombus. Compare measurements in correctly aligned end-diastolic views rather than including trabeculae or an oblique section.

Marked T-wave inversion is a useful clue but not a unique diagnosis. Coronary disease, other cardiomyopathies and relevant electrical or systemic causes must remain in the differential according to the presentation.

Use the Result to Assess More Than the Label

**An ultrasound-enhancing agent is a reasonable echo alternative when apical definition is inadequate, particularly if CMR is unavailable or contraindicated.** The question supplies feasible CMR, making it a direct comprehensive structural investigation.

Look for midventricular obstruction and an apical aneurysm; an aneurysm can create a distinct arrhythmic and thromboembolic problem. Apical phenotype alone should not be equated with universally benign prognosis.

Assess symptoms, rhythm, family history and the full HCM sudden-death framework after confirming anatomy. Treat a documented thrombus according to the indication, but do not assume every apical cavity shape requires anticoagulation. CMR complements echocardiographic hemodynamics and ambulatory rhythm assessment rather than replacing them. An enhancement pattern adds prognostic context but is not by itself proof of a particular causal variant. Explain why an apparently reassuring EF does not resolve a regional anatomical question, and ensure the eventual report describes the apex explicitly.

Invasive left ventriculography: Ventriculography can demonstrate cavity shape when catheterization is otherwise indicated. It adds procedural burden and does not provide the myocardial thickness and scar characterization available from CMR.

Transesophageal echocardiography: TEE is useful for valve anatomy and selected structural questions. The LV apex is relatively far from the probe, so it is not the preferred comprehensive test for this incompletely defined apical phenotype when CMR is feasible.

Exercise stress echocardiography: Exercise echo is important for latent obstruction and symptom physiology. It does not reliably solve an inadequate apical acoustic window or provide the same tissue characterization as CMR.

questions.question: A patient with HCM has exertional dyspnea attributable to a resting LVOT gradient of 72 mmHg. BP is 126/76 mmHg, EF is preserved, and there is no congestion, bronchospasm, marked bradycardia or AV block. No symptom-directed medication has been tried. Which initial strategy best follows the AHA/ACC 2024 pathway?
options: Titrate a nonvasodilating beta blocker to symptom benefit and tolerance
Start verapamil as initial monotherapy
Start disopyramide with AV nodal blockade as the initial regimen
Start a cardiac myosin inhibitor as the initial regimen
questions.explanation:
Initial Medication for Symptomatic Obstructive HCM

Correct answer: Titrate a nonvasodilating beta blocker to symptom benefit and tolerance

Reduce the Dynamic Obstructive Burden

**A nonvasodilating beta blocker is recommended for symptoms attributable to obstructive HCM.** Reduced adrenergic drive, slower rate and reduced contractility can improve filling and lessen obstruction.

Choose a suitable agent and titrate according to symptoms, pressure, heart rate, conduction and tolerance rather than treating a single resting pulse as the whole therapeutic endpoint. Review bronchospasm, advanced conduction disease and interactions.

The aim is symptom and physiological improvement; this prescription should not be presented as a proven replacement for indicated sudden-death protection.

Use Alternatives and Escalation With Safety Checks

**Verapamil or diltiazem can replace an ineffective or poorly tolerated beta blocker in suitable patients.** Avoid assuming that combining both nodal drug classes gives greater benefit without additional risk.

Verapamil can be harmful with hypotension, severe dyspnea at rest or very high resting gradients, particularly above one hundred millimeters of mercury. Reduced EF and conduction disease also change the drug balance.

Persistent important symptoms despite suitable first-line therapy warrant an experienced HCM assessment for a cardiac myosin inhibitor in an eligible adult, disopyramide with appropriate nodal blockade, or septal reduction. Diuretics can be used cautiously for genuine congestion, but excessive preload reduction may worsen obstruction; this stem supplies no congestion. Review medicines that lower afterload or increase contractility, hydration and triggers. Reassess symptoms and gradients after titration rather than escalating solely because the original gradient was high. A practical adult starting example is metoprolol succinate extended release ==25 mg== orally once daily, followed by monitored titration to symptom benefit and tolerance. This is a formulation-specific example, not a universal dose for every beta blocker.

Start verapamil as initial monotherapy: Verapamil is an appropriate alternative when a beta blocker is ineffective or not tolerated. In the named 2024 pathway, the suitable untreated patient first receives a nonvasodilating beta blocker.

Start disopyramide with AV nodal blockade as the initial regimen: This is an established escalation strategy for persistent obstructive symptoms. QT, renal and anticholinergic effects require assessment; it is not the first step in the specified untreated 2024-pathway presentation.

Start a cardiac myosin inhibitor as the initial regimen: Myosin inhibitors are effective treatment options, and newer monotherapy evidence has developed. The question explicitly asks for the 2024 pathway, which starts with an appropriate nonvasodilating beta blocker before its escalation choices.

questions.question: A patient with known obstructive HCM becomes hypotensive after volume depletion. Bedside echo shows a small hyperdynamic LV, systolic anterior mitral motion and a severe dynamic LVOT gradient; lungs are clear. After cautious IV fluid assessment and replacement, hypotension persists. Which vasoactive strategy is most appropriate?
options: Dobutamine to increase contractility of the hyperdynamic LV
A monitored vasoconstrictor without beta-inotropic activity, such as phenylephrine
Nitroprusside to reduce the pressure against which the LV ejects
IV loop diuretic escalation to shrink the hyperdynamic cavity
questions.explanation:
Acute Hypotension With Dynamic LVOT Obstruction

Correct answer: A monitored vasoconstrictor without beta-inotropic activity, such as phenylephrine

Identify the Mechanism Before Choosing Shock Treatment

**Dynamic LVOTO can cause low forward output despite a high EF.** Volume depletion, vasodilation, tachycardia and increased contractility can narrow the outflow region and intensify systolic anterior mitral motion.

Assess bleeding, infection, arrhythmia, ischemia and other causes concurrently. A known HCM diagnosis does not prove that every hypotensive episode is due to obstruction; the supplied echo identifies the mechanism here.

Replace a genuine volume deficit cautiously while monitoring lungs and filling. Fluid is not an unlimited prescription when congestion or another shock mechanism is present.

Support Filling and Afterload Without Increasing Inotropy

**AHA/ACC guidance recommends phenylephrine or another vasoconstrictor without inotropic activity when acute hypotension persists despite fluid administration.** Titrate under continuous hemodynamic monitoring.

Specialist beta blockade can sometimes be used with vasoconstrictor support to reduce contractility and obstruction. Do not extrapolate this into unmonitored beta-blocker administration in every shocked patient.

Review and withhold aggravating vasodilators or inotropes when clinically appropriate. Correct the precipitating volume loss and rhythm problem, then repeat echo and reassess perfusion rather than judging success from blood pressure alone. This differs from severe primary systolic pump failure, where selected inotropic support may be necessary. Mitral regurgitation caused by systolic anterior motion can improve as the obstructive physiology is corrected. The drug choice is determined by the demonstrated dynamic mechanism, not simply by the words cardiogenic shock. Escalate to an experienced critical-care and HCM team when perfusion remains inadequate or the diagnosis is mixed.

Dobutamine to increase contractility of the hyperdynamic LV: Dobutamine can support low-output systolic pump failure in selected settings. Here additional inotropy can intensify systolic anterior motion and dynamic obstruction, worsening forward flow.

Nitroprusside to reduce the pressure against which the LV ejects: Afterload reduction can improve selected severe regurgitant or hypertensive presentations. In this preload-depleted obstructive physiology it can worsen the outflow gradient and hypotension.

IV loop diuretic escalation to shrink the hyperdynamic cavity: Diuresis treats congestion when it is present. Further reducing preload in a small underfilled LV with clear lungs can aggravate obstruction rather than correct the mechanism of shock.

AHA/ACC multisociety hypertrophic cardiomyopathy guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.014

Escalation for Persistent Obstructive HCM Symptoms

Correct answer: Shared selection among myosin inhibition, disopyramide-based treatment and expert septal reduction

Confirm That Obstruction Explains the Limitation

**Persistent symptoms despite appropriate initial therapy and a significant resting or physiologically provoked gradient support advanced HCM assessment.** Recheck adherence, dose tolerance, loading conditions and competing causes of dyspnea.

The supplied gradient is above the usual fifty-millimeter threshold. Imaging must still define septal thickness, mitral anatomy, systolic anterior motion and the location of obstruction.

Discuss the patient’s goals, comorbidity, monitoring access and procedural preferences. A numerical gradient alone does not decide between medication and intervention.

Choose Among Supported Alternatives Rather Than a Mandatory Sequence

**The 2024 US pathway includes an eligible adult cardiac myosin inhibitor, disopyramide with AV nodal blockade, or septal reduction in an experienced service.** The balance depends on anatomy, contraindications, availability and preference.

Myosin inhibition requires EF surveillance and interaction review because excess negative inotropy can cause systolic dysfunction. Disopyramide requires QT, renal and anticholinergic assessment and appropriate nodal protection.

Myectomy can address anatomy that also requires mitral or other cardiac surgery. Alcohol ablation requires suitable septal arterial supply and is selected after procedural risk assessment, not from age or gradient alone. Explain the possibility of conduction block, pacemaker need and other procedural complications. Symptom improvement does not remove an independent ICD or AF-anticoagulation indication. Use the recommendation year explicitly; evolving drug approvals and labels need their own current checks before prescribing. Reassess the outcome after the chosen strategy rather than treating referral as the endpoint of care.

Add verapamil to the maximally tolerated beta blocker as the default escalation: Verapamil can replace a poorly tolerated or ineffective beta blocker in suitable patients. Routine dual nodal/negative-inotropic treatment is not the named default escalation and can cause bradycardia, conduction block and hypotension.

Require failure of disopyramide before discussing any myosin inhibitor or septal procedure: Disopyramide is a legitimate escalation option, but the named pathway does not require every patient to exhaust it before a shared discussion of the other supported alternatives.

Choose alcohol septal ablation before assessing septal and coronary anatomy: Alcohol ablation is appropriate in selected anatomy and clinical circumstances. Its safety and efficacy depend on a suitable target and broader procedural assessment; a high gradient alone does not establish that choice.

questions.question: A suitable surgical candidate has severely symptomatic obstructive HCM despite appropriate medication, a 92-mmHg provoked gradient and intrinsic degenerative mitral disease requiring repair. Which procedural strategy best addresses the supplied anatomy?
options: Alcohol septal ablation followed by reassessment of the intrinsic mitral lesion
Septal myectomy with appropriate mitral repair at an experienced HCM surgical center
Mitral repair without a septal procedure
Mitral valve replacement without septal reduction
questions.explanation:
Selecting Septal Myectomy When Other Surgery Is Needed

Correct answer: Septal myectomy with appropriate mitral repair at an experienced HCM surgical center

Match the Intervention to All Relevant Anatomy

**Myectomy is favored when obstructive HCM coexists with cardiac disease that independently requires surgery.** Intrinsic mitral disease, abnormal papillary anatomy, significant coronary disease or another surgical valve lesion can make a combined operation appropriate.

Distinguish intrinsic valve pathology from regurgitation caused mainly by systolic anterior motion. The latter may improve after adequate relief of obstruction without a separate valve replacement.

Review septal thickness, obstruction location, mitral apparatus and coronary anatomy through an experienced multidisciplinary team. Intraoperative imaging helps assess the result and residual mitral dysfunction.

Compare Septal Reduction Strategies

**Alcohol ablation requires a suitable septal arterial target and appropriate myocardial distribution.** It creates a controlled septal infarct and cannot correct every accompanying structural abnormality.

It is particularly relevant when severe symptoms persist and surgery is contraindicated or carries unacceptable risk, provided anatomy is suitable. Discuss heart block and pacemaker need as well as residual obstruction and repeat intervention.

Septal reduction requires important attributable symptoms, adequate dynamic obstruction and sufficient target anatomy. Neither a gradient alone nor a wish to prevent sudden death establishes the procedure indication. Do not replace a mitral valve solely to relieve LVOTO when an appropriate septal procedure can address the mechanism. Continue independent AF, HF and arrhythmic-risk assessment after successful surgery; symptom relief is not evidence that every disease-related risk has disappeared. The supplied valve lesion is a separate reason to choose a surgical strategy, rather than treating all high-gradient patients as interchangeable candidates for catheter ablation.

Alcohol septal ablation followed by reassessment of the intrinsic mitral lesion: Alcohol ablation can relieve obstruction in selected patients, especially when surgery is unsuitable. It does not repair an intrinsic degenerative valve lesion already requiring surgery, making a combined surgical approach more appropriate here.

Mitral repair without a septal procedure: Repair treats the intrinsic lesion, but does not reliably eliminate the separate septal mechanism producing severe LVOTO. Planning should address both anatomical contributors rather than assuming valve repair alone solves the outflow problem.

Mitral valve replacement without septal reduction: Replacement can be needed for genuinely nonrepairable intrinsic valve disease. Here repair is feasible and significant septal obstruction is present; replacing the valve to address outflow physiology is less suitable than tailored myectomy with repair.

questions.question: An adult with HCM has no previous arrest or sustained VT. Which finding is a major primary-prevention risk marker in the AHA/ACC 2024 framework?
options: LGE involving eighteen percent of LV mass
An LV apical aneurysm with transmural scar or LGE
Frequent, fast NSVT on ambulatory monitoring
Left atrial anteroposterior diameter of fifty millimeters
questions.explanation:
Major Adult HCM Sudden-Death Risk Markers

Correct answer: An LV apical aneurysm with transmural scar or LGE

Use the Named Adult Framework

**One or more major adult HCM risk markers supports offering an ICD discussion under AHA/ACC guidance.** This is primary prevention, distinct from an ICD recommendation after documented arrest or sustained ventricular arrhythmia.

Verify family circumstances, the nature of syncope and imaging measurements. A diagnostic feature such as mild wall thickening should not be promoted into a sudden-death marker without meeting the appropriate definition.

A scarred apical aneurysm is an arrhythmic substrate even when global EF is preserved. Its relevance is not removed by the absence of resting LVOTO.

Translate Risk Markers Into an Individual Decision

**Risk assessment requires shared discussion of arrhythmic risk, competing illness, device complications and patient preferences.** A marker supports an offer of protection; it does not predict that every untreated patient will experience an event.

Extensive LGE and NSVT can influence decisions when the major-marker assessment is inconclusive. The adult framework must not be copied unchanged into children, where measurements and risk models differ.

Repeat evaluation as the phenotype evolves and promptly investigate new syncope or sustained palpitations. A successful gradient treatment does not remove an independently relevant scar, prior event or family history. Device selection should consider pacing and ATP needs as well as the consequences of inappropriate shocks, lead problems and future replacements. Medical suppression of ventricular ectopy is not an equivalent substitute for an independently indicated ICD. Record which feature actually supports the discussion rather than labeling the patient high risk from the HCM diagnosis alone.

Major adult marker | Relevant definition

Familial HCM-related sudden death | First-degree or close relative aged ≤50 years; confirm attribution

Massive LV hypertrophy | Maximal segment thickness ==≥30 mm==

Recent likely arrhythmic syncope | Not explained by reflex mechanism or LVOTO

LV apical aneurysm | With transmural scar or LGE

LV systolic impairment | EF ==<50%==

LGE involving eighteen percent of LV mass: Extensive LGE can support ICD consideration when assessment remains uncertain, but the named adult framework treats it as additional evidence rather than one of the listed major markers.

Frequent, fast NSVT on ambulatory monitoring: NSVT is clinically relevant and greater burden or faster/longer runs increase concern. In the named adult framework it informs additional risk assessment rather than being classified as one of the major-marker list.

Left atrial anteroposterior diameter of fifty millimeters: LA size contributes to the HCM Risk-SCD model and can reflect disease burden. It is not a standalone major marker in the AHA/ACC adult list asked about here.

AHA/ACC multisociety hypertrophic cardiomyopathy guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.014

questions.question: An adult with HCM has an estimated five-year HCM Risk-SCD value of 3%, no major AHA/ACC risk marker and LGE involving approximately 18% of LV mass. The patient asks whether the numerical estimate makes further ICD discussion unnecessary. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Require inducible sustained VT at EPS before discussing an ICD
Exclude ICD consideration because the model estimate is below four percent
Treat LGE above fifteen percent as a mandatory ICD indication
Discuss the extensive scar as additional risk evidence; the low estimate does not end individualized ICD assessment
questions.explanation:
HCM Risk Models and Additional CMR Evidence

Correct answer: Discuss the extensive scar as additional risk evidence; the low estimate does not end individualized ICD assessment

Know What the Model Includes and Omits

**HCM Risk-SCD integrates age, maximal wall thickness, LA diameter, maximal LVOT gradient, family history, NSVT and unexplained syncope.** It estimates a five-year outcome in an appropriate population rather than measuring risk directly.

The conventional ESC risk bands are below ==4%==, 4 to below ==6%==, and at least ==6%==. They inform progressively stronger consideration of ICD therapy, while eligibility, clinical context and patient preference remain essential.

Do not use an adult model unchanged in children or assume perfect validation after every intervention or in every HCM phenocopy. Check the model’s intended setting before interpreting its output.

Interpret Scar as Additional Evidence

**Extensive LGE, commonly defined as at least ==15%== of LV mass, can support ICD consideration when conventional assessment is uncertain.** Measurement technique and the total phenotype affect interpretation.

AHA/ACC distinguishes its major adult risk markers from additional findings such as extensive scar or NSVT. ESC combines model-based estimation with additional clinical evidence; these frameworks should be named rather than merged into an invented score.

Explain the uncertainty of the absolute event estimate and the potential burdens of long-term device treatment. Scar burden is not a universal implantation mandate, but it should not be dismissed because an earlier calculation was low. Review rhythm monitoring and imaging quality, assess competing mortality and revisit the decision as new clinical features emerge. The defensible response is a renewed shared risk discussion, not automatic implantation from the scar number or automatic exclusion from the model number.

Require inducible sustained VT at EPS before discussing an ICD: EPS can answer selected arrhythmia questions, but inducibility is not a prerequisite in the standard HCM primary-prevention framework. A negative result would not erase the supplied imaging evidence.

Exclude ICD consideration because the model estimate is below four percent: A low model estimate informs assessment, but the model does not include every relevant scar or functional feature. Additional risk evidence can change the shared decision.

Treat LGE above fifteen percent as a mandatory ICD indication: Extensive scar supports a risk discussion in this setting, but does not create a universal implantation mandate. Expected benefit, competing risk, measurement quality and patient preference remain part of the decision.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man with established HCM has ECG-documented symptomatic paroxysmal AF. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is zero. There is no mechanical valve, significant mitral stenosis or anticoagulant contraindication. Which stroke-prevention strategy is appropriate?
options: Oral anticoagulation, with an appropriate DOAC preferred
No antithrombotic treatment until the conventional score reaches two
Aspirin as the initial alternative because the score is zero
Anticoagulation only during symptomatic episodes and the days immediately afterward
questions.explanation:
Anticoagulation for Clinical AF in HCM

Correct answer: Oral anticoagulation, with an appropriate DOAC preferred

Use the HCM-Specific Embolic-Risk Recommendation

**Clinical AF in HCM warrants oral anticoagulation independent of CHA2DS2-VASc.** AHA/ACC guidance prefers DOACs when suitable, with vitamin K antagonists as the alternative.

Choose the drug and dose using renal function, age, body weight, interactions and the relevant label. Mechanical valves and significant mitral stenosis create separate anticoagulant-selection rules; the stem excludes them.

Assess bleeding risk and correct modifiable contributors, but do not confuse a bleeding score with a reason to substitute aspirin for effective stroke prevention.

Distinguish Clinical AF From Short Device-Detected Episodes

**For subclinical AF lasting more than 24 hours in a single episode, the 2024 HCM guideline also recommends anticoagulation independent of the conventional score.** Shorter episodes need more individualized interpretation.

For episodes longer than five minutes but shorter than twenty-four hours, anticoagulation can be beneficial after considering burden, underlying risk and bleeding. Do not apply the same certainty to a brief unverified device signal.

Verify stored rhythm data when appropriate and address rate or rhythm control separately. Poorly tolerated AF can markedly impair filling in HCM and may justify cardioversion, antiarrhythmic therapy or ablation assessment. Restoration of sinus rhythm does not automatically remove the anticoagulation indication in a patient with established clinical AF. Review adherence and renal function and explain the difference between symptom control and embolic protection. The key distinction here is the disease-specific context: a score of zero does not overrule the supplied HCM-associated clinical AF.

No antithrombotic treatment until the conventional score reaches two: HCM-associated clinical AF has a disease-specific anticoagulation recommendation independent of the conventional score. Waiting for additional score components can leave a relevant embolic risk untreated.

Aspirin as the initial alternative because the score is zero: Aspirin is not an equivalent substitute for indicated anticoagulation in HCM with clinical AF. A low conventional score does not create an aspirin-first pathway for this disease.

Anticoagulation only during symptomatic episodes and the days immediately afterward: Intermittent symptoms do not reliably identify all AF exposure or thromboembolic risk. Long-term prevention is based on the established HCM-AF context, not an unvalidated symptom-triggered dosing schedule.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

Use the HCM-Specific Embolic-Risk Recommendation

  • Clinical AF in HCM warrants oral anticoagulation independent of CHA2DS2-VASc. AHA/ACC guidance prefers DOACs when suitable, with vitamin K antagonists as the alternative.
    • Choose the drug and dose using renal function, age, body weight, interactions and the relevant label. Mechanical valves and significant mitral stenosis create separate anticoagulant-selection rules; the stem excludes them.
    • Assess bleeding risk and correct modifiable contributors, but do not confuse a bleeding score with a reason to substitute aspirin for effective stroke prevention.

Distinguish Clinical AF From Short Device-Detected Episodes

  • For subclinical AF lasting more than 24 hours in a single episode, the 2024 HCM guideline also recommends anticoagulation independent of the conventional score. Shorter episodes need more individualized interpretation.
    • For episodes longer than five minutes but shorter than twenty-four hours, anticoagulation can be beneficial after considering burden, underlying risk and bleeding. Do not apply the same certainty to a brief unverified device signal.
    • Verify stored rhythm data when appropriate and address rate or rhythm control separately. Poorly tolerated AF can markedly impair filling in HCM and may justify cardioversion, antiarrhythmic therapy or ablation assessment. Restoration of sinus rhythm does not automatically remove the anticoagulation indication in a patient with established clinical AF. Review adherence and renal function and explain the difference between symptom control and embolic protection. The key distinction here is the disease-specific context: a score of zero does not overrule the supplied HCM-associated clinical AF.

Other Options

  • B — No antithrombotic treatment until the conventional score reaches two: HCM-associated clinical AF has a disease-specific anticoagulation recommendation independent of the conventional score. Waiting for additional score components can leave a relevant embolic risk untreated.
  • C — Aspirin as the initial alternative because the score is zero: Aspirin is not an equivalent substitute for indicated anticoagulation in HCM with clinical AF. A low conventional score does not create an aspirin-first pathway for this disease.
  • D — Anticoagulation only during symptomatic episodes and the days immediately afterward: Intermittent symptoms do not reliably identify all AF exposure or thromboembolic risk. Long-term prevention is based on the established HCM-AF context, not an unvalidated symptom-triggered dosing schedule.

  • AHA/ACC multisociety hypertrophic cardiomyopathy guideline, 2024
  • ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023

questions.question: A patient with established HCM develops persistent exertional limitation and LVEF 44%. Resting and provoked imaging show no significant LVOTO. Coronary assessment finds no explanatory disease. Which management interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Add disopyramide to the symptom-control regimen
Continue symptom treatment and reassess EF before initiating the systolic-HF pathway
Treat the new systolic dysfunction and reassess advanced-HF and ICD needs using the HCM framework
Refer for septal reduction to improve exertional dyspnea
questions.explanation:
Systolic Dysfunction in Established HCM

Correct answer: Treat the new systolic dysfunction and reassess advanced-HF and ICD needs using the HCM framework

Recognize the Disease-Specific EF Threshold

**Persistent LVEF below ==50%== represents systolic dysfunction in HCM.** A patient whose earlier EF was hyperdynamic can have clinically important decline before reaching conventional severe-HFrEF thresholds.

Reassess for coronary disease, tachyarrhythmia, valvular disease, drug effects and other contributors rather than assuming every deterioration is irreversible HCM progression.

Repeat reliable imaging when a single unexpected value is uncertain and assess congestion, perfusion, rhythm and functional limitation. A disappearing gradient can reflect altered contractility rather than successful disease modification.

Change the Treatment Objective

**Use guideline-directed systolic-HF treatment as appropriate and review negative inotropes.** The 2024 guidance calls for discontinuing cardiac myosin inhibitors when persistent systolic dysfunction develops.

Verapamil, diltiazem and disopyramide can become unsuitable as the physiology changes. Continue individually indicated therapies after assessing pressure, conduction, renal function and tolerability rather than retaining an obstruction regimen by habit.

EF below fifty is also a major adult HCM sudden-death risk marker, supporting an ICD discussion before simply importing the usual thirty-five-percent rule. Evaluate CRT when the electrical and clinical criteria support it, and refer for advanced-HF or transplant assessment when severe limitation persists despite appropriate care. Some HCM patients have advanced HF even with preserved EF because of restrictive filling or a small cavity; EF is not the sole referral criterion. Reassess rhythm and anticoagulation needs and explain why a treatment that helped earlier obstructive physiology may no longer fit the current presentation.

Add disopyramide to the symptom-control regimen: Disopyramide is used to reduce obstruction in suitable patients. Additional negative inotropy is not the appropriate response to nonobstructive systolic dysfunction.

Continue symptom treatment and reassess EF before initiating the systolic-HF pathway: In HCM, an EF below fifty percent signifies systolic dysfunction. Waiting for thirty-five percent misses an important disease-specific change and its risk implications.

Refer for septal reduction to improve exertional dyspnea: Septal reduction can improve symptoms due to drug-refractory dynamic obstruction in suitable anatomy. The supplied nonobstructive phenotype with reduced EF instead requires assessment and treatment of systolic myocardial failure.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

questions.question: A 16-year-old carries the family’s established pathogenic HCM variant. There are no symptoms, ECG abnormalities or imaging evidence of HCM. The family asks about follow-up and competitive sport. Which plan best fits AHA/ACC 2024 guidance?
options: Allow recreational activity but exclude competitive sport on genotype alone
Repeat cardiac assessment only if symptoms develop
Start preventive beta blockade and defer repeat imaging until adulthood
Continue serial phenotype surveillance with individualized sports assessment
questions.explanation:
Genotype-Positive Relatives and Exercise Counseling

Correct answer: Continue serial phenotype surveillance with individualized sports assessment

Follow the Age-Dependent Phenotype

**A genotype-positive, phenotype-negative relative needs serial clinical assessment, ECG and cardiac imaging.** The 2024 US intervals are generally every one to two years in children and adolescents and every three to five years in adults.

Assess sooner for syncope, exertional chest discomfort, sustained palpitations or a change in the family history. Routine intervals are not instructions to defer evaluation of new symptoms.

Confirm that the familial result is pathogenic or likely pathogenic in an established disease gene. A VUS does not provide an equivalent basis for labeling a healthy person a confirmed carrier.

Counsel Activity Without Treating Genotype as Disease Severity

**Competitive sport is reasonable for genotype-positive individuals without the HCM phenotype under the 2024 framework.** Discuss the person’s evaluation, sport demands and the plan for ongoing follow-up.

Established HCM needs its own exercise and risk assessment. Mild-to-moderate recreational activity is generally beneficial; vigorous or competitive activity requires the applicable expert review and shared discussion rather than a blanket rule for every patient.

An ICD is not a sports eligibility device and should follow an independent clinical indication. Discuss symptom reporting and practical emergency planning without promising zero risk or predicting inevitable disease. A reassuring current assessment supports activity decisions in the present, while surveillance addresses possible later expression. Changes in imaging, symptoms or arrhythmia can require revisiting participation. Separate transmission risk, penetrance and clinical severity during counseling so a molecular result does not become an unsupported prediction of the teenager’s future functional capacity.

Allow recreational activity but exclude competitive sport on genotype alone: Guidance allows genotype-positive, phenotype-negative individuals to participate in competitive sport. Assessment and counseling remain appropriate, but genotype alone does not create a universal exclusion rule.

Repeat cardiac assessment only if symptoms develop: A pathogenic carrier can remain asymptomatic while the phenotype evolves. Scheduled adolescent surveillance remains appropriate; symptom-triggered review supplements rather than replaces it.

Start preventive beta blockade and defer repeat imaging until adulthood: Beta blockade has symptom and arrhythmia roles in clinically expressed HCM, but is not established as a substitute for surveillance in a phenotype-negative carrier. The adolescent still needs periodic imaging and clinical review.

questions.question: A stable adult has newly recognized LV dilatation and LVEF 31%. Coronary and valve assessment does not explain the dysfunction. There is no shock, high-grade AV block or sustained ventricular arrhythmia. Baseline clinical and laboratory assessment has begun. Which additional investigation most broadly refines the myocardial phenotype before selecting more targeted tests?
options: Broad serum viral antibody testing
CMR with ventricular assessment and tissue characterization
Endomyocardial biopsy
Cardiac FDG-PET
questions.explanation:
Etiological Assessment of Newly Diagnosed DCM

Correct answer: CMR with ventricular assessment and tissue characterization

Characterize the Phenotype and Search for a Cause

**DCM requires ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction not explained solely by abnormal loading conditions or coronary disease.** Once the phenotype is recognized, evaluate inherited and acquired contributors rather than treating idiopathic as the starting conclusion.

CMR evaluates chamber function, nonischemic scar, regional abnormalities and clues to inflammation, iron or infiltration. Interpretation must integrate the clinical presentation; a pattern is not a standalone proof of a gene or pathogen.

Obtain a detailed pedigree and review alcohol, cardiotoxic treatment, sustained tachycardia, pregnancy timing, endocrine/metabolic disease and extracardiac findings. Initial laboratory testing and rhythm assessment should be directed by the clinical context.

Reserve Specialized Tests for a Defined Decision

**Biopsy is most useful when tissue diagnosis is expected to alter management.** Shock, important conduction disease, malignant arrhythmia, progressive dysfunction or a specific treatable histological suspicion can change the urgency and sequencing.

FDG-PET answers selected questions about inflammatory activity and distribution; it requires preparation that suppresses physiological uptake. Broad viral antibody positivity does not establish a myocardial viral diagnosis or justify antiviral treatment.

Consider genetic counseling and phenotype-directed testing when results can clarify cause, risk or family care, including presentations without an obvious positive pedigree. Begin appropriate HF treatment in parallel rather than postponing care until every etiological test returns. Reassess EF after therapy and investigate new arrhythmia or syncope promptly. This question asks for broad myocardial characterization in a stable patient, not a rule that CMR must precede biopsy in every fulminant or high-risk presentation.

Broad serum viral antibody testing: Viral serology often reflects prior systemic exposure and does not reliably establish infection within myocardium. Targeted infection testing can be appropriate, but a broad antibody panel is not the general etiological solution.

Endomyocardial biopsy: Biopsy can change urgent care in high-risk or specifically suspected inflammatory/infiltrative disease. This stable presentation does not make routine biopsy before a suitable CMR the preferred broad next step.

Cardiac FDG-PET: FDG-PET is useful for selected inflammatory questions such as cardiac sarcoidosis when properly prepared. It is not the universal first myocardial characterization test for every stable unexplained DCM presentation.

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

ESC myocarditis and pericarditis guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192

EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS genetic testing consensus, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1002/joa3.12717
